summary: Martian Map is a working web prototype of a NASA-style mission control for Mars, built from the Interplanetary Survival Guide brief. It combines a 3D globe and 2D map, seven toggleable layers, a five-briefing dashboard, a mission planner and a survival simulation in one self-contained HTML page, with a matching 13-slide presentation. A catalogue of 33 sites covers 25 documented Martian locations and 8 proposed, simulated facilities. Every value carries one of five classes: confirmed observation, derived measurement, interpretation, hypothesis or simulated data. Ice deposits are never presented as accessible water, and no route is ever called safe. The planner compares three modeled routes by distance, ascent, steep terrain and travel time, then writes a copyable report. Survival mode shows how dust, season, crew and solar area change power, battery, water and food. The main limit is that terrain, weather and survival numbers come from demonstration models, not NASA measurements, and live data, the backend and the Android app are not built. The interface also still needs testing in real browsers and on phones. Catalogue coordinates must still be verified against NASA sources. Next steps are real elevation and imagery, live weather, saved missions and Android packaging. Is
details:
1. Project overview • Project name: Interplanetary Survival Guide, Martian Map. • Subtitle: The First Human Expedition to Mars. • Tagline: Explore the Unknown. Survive the Red Planet. Discover the Future. • Project type in the brief: an advanced interactive planetary exploration and survival application. • Platforms in the brief: a web application and an Android application. • Design direction in the brief: realistic NASA Mission Control. • Primary objective in the brief: an immersive, scientifically informative and interactive system that shows how humans could explore, study and prepare for survival on Mars. • What was built: a working web prototype delivered as one self-contained HTML page of about 74 KB. • Companion deliverable: a 13-slide presentation, also available as a PDF. • Companion deliverable: a project report, of which this document is the detailed version. • The supplied brief is cut off partway through section 14, on performance, security and reliability. • The prototype and this report follow sections 1 to 13 of the brief. • The application is a mission-planning and educational simulation, not an operational or life-support system. • The application is meant to feel like a professional planetary research platform, not a conventional educational website. 2. Objectives and scope Objectives from the brief • Create a realistic and interactive 3D representation of Mars. Status: partly met, as a stylized procedural globe. • Integrate authentic public NASA and planetary science data. Status: partly met, through a catalogue of published site coordinates. • Identify scientifically documented water-ice resources. Status: met, with 7 ice sites in 4 evidence classes. • Visualise environmental conditions and geographical hazards. Status: partly met, using modeled weather and hazards. • Let users create and compare hypothetical exploration routes. Status: met, with 3 modeled routes per trip. • Simulate astronaut survival and mission planning. Status: met, with 5 labeled simulation modules. • Provide detailed scientific information about important locations. Status: met, with panels for 33 sites. • Deliver a consistent experience across desktop, mobile and Android. Status: partly met, as a responsive touch-ready web page with no Android build. • Tally: four objectives fully met and four partly met. In scope • One single-page web application. • The 3D globe and the 2D map. • Seven map layers. • Search, bookmarks, recent items, share and export. • The selected-location dashboard. • The mission planner. • Survival mode. • Charts with units and hover readouts. • A settings and data-sources page. • The 13-slide presentation and the project reports. Out of scope for this prototype • Live calls to NASA services. • Real imagery and real elevation tiles. • The FastAPI backend. • The PostgreSQL and PostGIS database. • User accounts. • The packaged Android application. 3. Visual design and navigation Colors • Rusty red and Martian orange as the main accents. • Burnt copper and sandy gold for highlights. • Deep charcoal and black for panels and background. • Muted grey and metallic silver for secondary text. • Subtle white and amber for emphasis. • Neon colors and cartoon-style graphics are avoided. Interface style • Semi-transparent glass-like panels with a background blur. • Subtle scan-line effect over the globe stage. • Animated coordinate readout that updates as the pointer moves over the surface. • Headings in Space Grotesk and coordinates and data in IBM Plex Mono. • A visible keyboard focus outline on controls. • Animation limited to a slow globe spin and a pulsing selection ring. • Animation stops when the viewer prefers reduced motion. Layout • Top bar with the title, a search box and a UTC clock with a reference sol. • Left rail with the main navigation. • Large central stage with the globe. • Right-hand panel with the selected-location dashboard. • On narrow screens the layout stacks into one column and the rail becomes a scrolling tab bar. The nine navigation sections • Mission Overview: purpose, catalogue counts, data classes and route labels. • Explore Mars: the globe or map itself. • Resource Mapping: every ice site with its evidence class and source. • Weather and Environment: charts comparing two sites over a chosen range. • Mission Planner: route planning and the mission report. • Astronaut Survival: the survival simulation. • Scientific Discoveries: a ten-event timeline and filterable site entries. • NASA Missions: rovers and landers, with orbiters listed separately. • Settings and Data Sources: intended sources, their status, and notes on going live and on Android. 4. The 3D and 2D explorer 3D globe construction • Built with Three.js release 128, loaded from a content delivery network. • The planet is a sphere of 96 by 64 segments. • The surface texture is a 512 by 256 pixel canvas, painted from 131,072 elevation samples at start-up. • Lighting is one ambient light at 0.62 and one warm directional light at 0.85. • A soft orange atmosphere glow is drawn as a slightly larger back-facing shell with an additive shader. • A field of 500 stars sits on a distant shell. • The camera has a 38 degree field of view. • Rendering resolution is capped at twice the device pixel ratio. 3D interaction • Drag with a mouse or one finger to rotate in all directions. • Tilt is limited to about 1.4 radians so the globe cannot flip over. • Scroll the mouse wheel or pinch with two fingers to zoom. • Zoom runs from 1.5 to 6 planet radii, starting at 3.4. • Rotation sensitivity scales with zoom so dragging feels the same near and far. • The globe turns slowly on its own until the user first touches it. • Reset view returns the camera and resumes the slow spin. • Moving the pointer over the surface updates a live readout of latitude, longitude and model elevation. • A click or tap selects the nearest visible marker within a distance that grows with zoom, at least 2 degrees of arc. • If no marker is near, the click selects an unnamed surface point. • Selecting a point shows a pulsing ring on the globe. • Search results and links fly the camera to the chosen place, tilting by 0.9 times its latitude. • On load the camera flies to Jezero Crater. Marker shapes • Ice sites: diamonds, colored by evidence class. • Proposed infrastructure: blue cubes. • Mission sites: rust-colored cones. • Discovery zones: gold spheres. 2D map • A flat equirectangular map showing the same texture, markers and routes. • A graticule is drawn every 30 degrees with degree labels. • Drag to pan and scroll or pinch to zoom from 1 to 12 times. • Marker names appear once zoom passes 1.4. • Click or tap selects the nearest marker or a surface point. • The 2D and 3D buttons switch views, and the selection carries across. • The 2D map is the automatic fallback if 3D cannot start. 5. Map layers A layer panel on the stage switches each layer on or off independently. The weather overlay starts off and the other six start on. Layer 1: Terrain and elevation • Colors the surface by elevation, blended 55 percent with the base surface color. • Ramp stops: minus 8 km deep blue-purple, minus 4 blue, minus 1 green, plus 1 yellow, plus 4 orange, plus 10 red, plus 21 white. • Adds hill shading from neighboring heights so relief reads clearly. • Whitens the poles above 80 degrees latitude. • Shows large formations such as Olympus Mons, the Tharsis volcanoes, Hellas and craters. • Slope and terrain class are computed on demand for the dashboard and routes, not drawn as a separate overlay. • The only landing area shown is the proposed LZ-1, in the infrastructure layer. Layer 2: Water and ice • Shows 7 ice-related sites as diamonds. • Green marks a confirmed observation. • Gold marks a derived measurement. • Amber marks an interpretation. • Red marks a hypothesis. • Every marker shows its evidence class and its source in its panel. • Ancient river channels and water-related formations appear through Kasei Valles and the Valles hydrated minerals. Layer 3: Weather overlay • Tints the surface from cool blue to warm orange by latitude. • Labeled simulated, because it comes from the demonstration weather model. • Detailed charts live in the Weather and Environment view. Layer 4: Exploration routes • Historical rover drives are solid orange lines. • The Curiosity and Perseverance routes are coarse three-point sketches, not surveyed drive traces, and say so. • A visually suggested traverse from HAB-A to RELAY-1 is a dashed pale line. • Routes from the planner are dashed lines in gold, light blue and lilac. Layer 5: Scientific discovery zones • Shows 9 geological features as gold spheres. • Each opens a panel with geology, significance, missions, source and date. Layer 6: Survival infrastructure • Shows 8 proposed facilities as blue cubes. • All are labeled proposed or simulated, because no such facility exists. Layer 7: NASA mission sites • Shows 9 landing sites as rust cones, covering NASA and partner missions. • Mission pages also list orbiters, which have no fixed surface location. 6. Site catalogue Counts • 33 sites in total. • 9 discovery zones. • 7 water and ice sites. • 9 mission sites. • 8 proposed facilities. • 25 documented sites and 8 simulated placeholders. Fields stored for each site • Identifier and name. • Latitude and longitude in degrees, east positive. • Layer. • Data class. • Feature type. • Published elevation, approximate and marked with a tilde. • Geological description. • Scientific significance. • Related missions. • Source. • Observation date. Discovery zones (latitude, longitude) • Olympus Mons, 18.65, -133.8, confirmed. A shield volcano and the largest known in the solar system. • Valles Marineris, -13.9, -59, confirmed. A canyon system about 4,000 km long. • Gale Crater, -5.4, 137.8, confirmed. Impact crater with a layered mound, Mount Sharp. • Jezero Crater, 18.4, 77.7, confirmed. Crater holding an ancient river delta. • Elysium Planitia, 3, 154.7, confirmed. Young volcanic plain. • Hellas Planitia, -42.4, 70.5, confirmed. Deep impact basin with the highest surface pressure on the planet. • Tharsis Montes, 1, -112, confirmed. Arsia, Pavonis and Ascraeus Mons. • Kasei Valles, 24, -65, interpretation. Outflow channel carved by large floods. • Olympia Undae dunes, 80, 180, confirmed. North polar dune field. Water and ice sites • Phoenix landing site, 68.2, -125.7, confirmed. First in-situ confirmation of ground ice. • North polar layered deposits, 86, 0, confirmed. Largest surface water ice reservoir. • South polar cap, -87, 0, confirmed. Carbon dioxide ice over water ice. • Utopia Planitia buried ice, 46, 118, interpretation. Radar and landform evidence, with depth and purity unknown. • Odyssey hydrogen-rich ground, 62, -60, derived. Neutron data poleward of about 60 degrees. • South polar subglacial reflections, -81, 193, hypothesis. Contested radar reflections, not a resource. • Valles hydrated minerals, -8, -76, interpretation. Water bound in minerals. Mission sites • Curiosity, -4.59, 137.44, landed 2012-08-06. • Perseverance, 18.44, 77.45, landed 2021-02-18. • InSight, 4.5, 135.62, landed 2018-11-26. • Zhurong, 25.07, 109.93, landed 2021-05-14. • Spirit, -14.57, 175.47, landed 2004-01-04. • Opportunity, -1.95, -5.53, landed 2004-01-25. • Viking 1, 22.27, -47.95, landed 1976-07-20. • Viking 2, 47.64, 134.26, landed 1976-09-03. • Mars Pathfinder, 19.13, -33.22, landed 1997-07-04. Proposed facilities, all simulated • HAB-A habitat, 18.2, 77.2, near Jezero. • HAB-B habitat, -4.3, 137.1, near Gale. • SOLAR-A solar field, 17.9, 77.9. • ISRU-1 resource processing, 19, 78.3. • RELAY-1 communications relay, 12, 95. • RELAY-2 communications relay, 6, 125. • SHELTER-1 emergency shelter, 16, 88. • LZ-1 landing zone, 18, 76.5. Orbiters listed • Mars Odyssey, arrived 2001. • Mars Express, 2003. • Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, 2006. • MAVEN, 2014. Accuracy notes • Coordinates are rounded published values written from general knowledge. • They have not been checked live against NASA sources and must be verified before real use. • The longitude 193 is stored as given and equals minus 167 east. 7. Dashboard, search and tools Header card • Location name, or Surface point for an unnamed spot. • Data class tag for named sites. • Latitude and longitude. • Model elevation in km and model slope in degrees. • Terrain class. • Nearest proposed habitat and its distance in km. • Buttons to set the point as a route start or destination. Terrain classes, from the model • Steep relief: slope above 10 degrees. • High volcanic highland: height above 8 km. • Southern highlands: height above 1 km. • Deep basin or canyon: height below minus 5 km. • Northern lowland plain: height below minus 2 km. • Rocky transitional plain: everything else. Five intelligence cards • Location Intelligence: published geology, feature type, published elevation, observation date and source. Unnamed points say the class comes from the demonstration model. • Resource Intelligence: up to four ice-related sites within 600 km with distances, plus a reminder that ice evidence is not an accessible water supply. • Environmental Intelligence: maximum and minimum surface temperature in kelvin, pressure in pascals, wind speed and direction, dust opacity, solar longitude and freshness. Each is labeled simulated for the model sol, not live. • Mission Intelligence: nearby rovers, landers and discoveries within 600 km. • Exploration Intelligence: a hazard list and a pointer to the planner. • A closing note says that one point's values do not describe the whole planet. Hazards flagged • Steep slopes above 8 degrees, from the model. • Polar cold and darkness poleward of 60 degrees. • High altitude and thin air above 8 km. • Deep basin and dust accumulation below minus 6 km. • Elevated dust opacity above 1.2, simulated. • Limited data coverage, always shown. Search • One search box in the top bar with name suggestions. • Matches site name, feature type, layer, data class, mission and significance text. • Accepts typed coordinates such as 18.4, 77.7. • Enter flies to the first match and reports how many matched. • A message appears when nothing matches. Other tools • Layer filtering through the layer panel. • Mission filtering by All, Rovers, Landers or Orbiters. • Discovery filtering by All, Geology or Resources. • Coordinate inspection by hover readout and by click. • Bookmarks for named markers, saved in the browser. • Recently viewed list of the last six sites. • Reset view button. • Share button, which copies the location name and coordinates as text. • Export button, which shows a copyable text briefing of the selection. • Distances are shown in the planner and the dashboard. A drag-to-measure ruler was not built. 8. Mission planner Workflow, as the brief lists it • Select a starting location from a menu or from the dashboard. • Select a destination the same way. • Display the geographic distance for each route. • Examine terrain through an elevation profile and statistics. • Activate related layers: the planner switches the routes layer on. • Identify hazards through the steep-terrain share and the maximum slope. • Explore alternatives through three candidate routes. • View nearby scientific sites through a count and a list in the report. • Estimate duration from stated assumptions. • Generate a mission report. Inputs • Start and destination. • Travel speed in km per hour, default 8. • Driving hours per sol, default 6. • A Compute routes button. Route generation • Route 1: the direct great-circle path. • Route 2: a northern detour. • Route 3: a southern detour. • Detours bend around the midpoint by 22 percent of the angular separation. • Each segment is sampled at 40 points. • The map flies to the midpoint and draws all three routes in different colors. Metrics per route • Total distance in km, using a Mars radius of 3,389.5 km. • Total ascent and descent in km. • Elevation range. • Maximum coarse slope in degrees. • Percentage of steep samples above 8 degrees. • Number of catalogue sites within 300 km. • Estimated travel time in sols. • Status, always modeled. Travel time • Base time is distance divided by speed times driving hours per sol. • The base is stretched by up to 2.5 times for the share of steep samples. • This is a planning assumption and not a vehicle model. Route status labels • Visually suggested: drawn by hand with no terrain check. • Modeled: computed on the demonstration terrain. All planner routes are this. • Validated: checked against surveyed data. No route is validated. • No route is ever called safe. Charts in the planner • Elevation profile with one line per route. • Route distance comparison as bars. Mission report fields • Mission name. • Start coordinates. • Destination coordinates. • Selected route and its status. • Total distance. • Estimated duration with the speed and hours used. • Terrain statistics. • Simulated environment at the route midpoint. • Potential challenges. • Nearby documented sites with their data classes. • Data sources. • Planning assumptions. • A not-for-operational-use line. Report delivery • The report appears as text with a copy button. • Printing and file download are blocked inside the hosted page, so the user copies the text into a document. 9. Survival simulation Labeling • A banner at the top states that all habitat readings, inventories and calculations are invented for teaching. • A card states that it is not a certified life-support or safety system. Scenario controls • Habitat site: HAB-A, HAB-B, the Phoenix landing site or Gale Crater. • Season as solar longitude from 0 to 360 degrees. • Dust opacity from 0.3 to 5. • Crew size from 2 to 8 people. • Solar array area from 100 to 600 square meters. • Preset Nominal: opacity 0.6 at solar longitude 90. • Preset Regional storm: opacity 2 at solar longitude 250. • Preset Global storm: opacity 4.5 at solar longitude 260. Module A: Habitat monitoring • Simulated cabin pressure of 70.3 kPa. • Simulated cabin temperature of 21 degrees Celsius. • Power generation, power load and battery level. • Mission progress shown as sol 30 of 500. Module B: Energy management • Daily mean sunlight at the top of the atmosphere from latitude, season and the changing Sun distance. • Surface sunlight after dust, using a transmission of 0.15 plus 0.85 times the exponential of minus 0.9 times opacity. • Array efficiency of 22 percent. • Power load of 8 kW plus 2.5 kW per crew member. • A chart of generated power across the Mars year against the load line. Module C: Resource management • Battery charge from the surplus or deficit, clamped between 0 and 100 percent. • A random day-to-day variation of plus or minus 10 percent in generation, from a fixed seed so results repeat. • Water starts at 60 liters per crew member and falls by 3.5 liters per person per sol. • Simulated ice mining adds up to 40 liters per sol from surplus power. • Food starts at 120 days and falls by one day's supply per sol. • A 30-sol chart of battery percent, water days and food days. Module D: Communication monitoring • Distance to the nearest proposed relay. • Link availability of 100 percent minus the distance in km divided by 20, kept between 0 and 100. • A weak-link warning below 40 percent. Module E: Environmental alerts • Dust: critical above opacity 2.5, a watch above 1.2. • Cold nights below 160 kelvin. • Steep terrain above 8 degrees. • Power deficit. • Battery below 20 percent at the end of the run. • Weak relay link. • A standing note that local observations are limited. Environment shown • External temperature range in kelvin. • Pressure in pascals. • Daily sunlight at the top of the atmosphere and at the surface in W per square meter. • Distance to the nearest relay. • Communication availability. Interactivity • Releasing any control re-runs the model and redraws the dashboard and charts. 10. Data integrity and classification The five classes

• Confirmed observation: measured directly. Example: Phoenix digging into ground ice. • Derived measurement: computed from instrument data. Example: Mars Odyssey hydrogen-rich ground. • Interpretation: scientists' reading of evidence. Example: buried ice in Utopia Planitia. • Hypothesis: proposed and debated. Example: possible liquid water under the south polar cap. • Simulated data: invented for planning and teaching. Example: proposed habitats and modeled weather. • Each class has its own color on tags, markers and charts. Rules enforced in the interface • Nothing is fabricated and presented as a NASA measurement. • Illustrative information is never presented as authentic scientific data. • A possible resource is never shown as a confirmed accessible water supply. • Every ice marker shows its evidence class and its source. • The south polar radar reflection is shown as a contested hypothesis. • One site's weather is never presented as planetary conditions. • Environmental values show units, a model sol and a not-live notice. • Where live data is unavailable, a notice says so and labeled demonstration data is used. • Proposed infrastructure is always labeled proposed or simulated. • No route is called safe, and none is labeled validated. • Survival results are labeled simulation and not operational advice. What is real and what is modeled • Site names, coordinates, mission names and dates: published values, rounded, entered from general knowledge. • Published elevations on site panels: approximate and marked with a tilde. • Surface texture and elevation grid: a procedural model, simulated. • Temperature, pressure, wind and dust: demonstration weather model, simulated. • Solar power, habitats, reserves and relays: survival simulation, simulated. • Routes and travel times: computed on the model terrain, modeled. Data-management items from the brief • Retrieve datasets: not built, because a hosted page cannot call NASA services. • Process measurements: done for the built-in models. • Organise by location and mission: every record carries coordinates and a mission list, and missions can be filtered. • Convert coordinates to the mapping system: latitude and longitude convert to 3D sphere points and to flat map positions. • Display through the correct layers: each record belongs to one layer. • Store metadata: source, date, class and type are kept per record. • Show timestamps: observation dates appear on site panels and model sols on environment values. • Handle missing information: notices explain what is unavailable. • Cache datasets: not applicable until live data exists. Only bookmarks are stored, in the browser. • Identify outdated observations: all environment values are marked as model, not live. Verification still required • Every catalogue coordinate and elevation must be checked against NASA, USGS or ESA references before real use. 11. Models and implementation details Terrain model • Elevation is a sum of several parts. • A north-south trend of minus 1.8 km times the sine of latitude, which makes the north lower. • Three scales of smooth value noise for relief. • Twelve large Gaussian bumps and basins at the positions of Olympus Mons, Tharsis, Hellas and other big features. • 110 randomly placed craters with a bowl and a raised rim, from a fixed seed so the surface is the same every time. • Unit vectors and cosine cutoffs are precomputed so each lookup skips far-away features. • In a test of 20,000 random points the heights ranged from about minus 7.0 to plus 19.4 km. • Olympus Mons measured about plus 19.6 km and Hellas about minus 6.6 km. • The model is not a measured surface. Surface texture • Each pixel starts from a rusty base color with noise. • Dark albedo patches are added from a second noise field. • Hill shading uses the heights of the four neighboring pixels. • The elevation ramp is blended at 55 percent when the terrain layer is on. • Poles are whitened above 80 degrees latitude. • A temperature tint is blended at 35 percent when the weather layer is on. • The texture is rebuilt whenever a layer that affects it is toggled. Slope • Finite differences over 0.4 degrees of latitude and longitude. • Converted to degrees. • Used for terrain class, hazard flags and the steep share of a route. • Coarse by design. Weather model • Mean temperature starts at 214 K plus 34 K scaled by the cosine of latitude, with a small seasonal term by hemisphere and a drop with altitude. • The day-night swing is 48 K, reduced by up to 35 percent under heavy dust. • Dust opacity has a base of 0.55 and rises in the dusty season near solar longitude 250, varying by place. • Pressure is 610 Pa at the reference level, falling exponentially with height on an 11.1 km scale height, with a seasonal swing of about 12 percent. • Wind speed is 3 to 10 m/s and direction is 0 to 360 degrees, from smooth noise. • One Mars year is 668.6 sols and solar longitude is the fraction of the year times 360 degrees. Routing mathematics • Points are interpolated along great circles on the sphere. • Distance is the sum of arc lengths times the Mars radius of 3,389.5 km. • Ascent and descent sum the positive and negative height changes between samples. • Steep share is checked on every fourth sample. • Nearby sites are collected within 300 km along the route. Solar mathematics • Solar declination is calculated from an axial tilt of 25.19 degrees and the season. • Orbital eccentricity of 0.0934 changes the Sun distance across the year. • The solar constant at Mars is scaled from 1,361 W per square meter by the squared Sun distance. • Daily mean sunlight comes from the day length at the chosen latitude. • Polar night and midnight sun are handled. Resilience • If WebGL cannot start, the app shows the 2D map and says so. • Browser storage reads and writes are wrapped so a blocked store does not break the page. • Copy buttons show a message if the clipboard is refused. • Charts and models need no network. Packaging • One HTML file of about 74 KB. • Three.js is loaded from a content delivery network, so the first load needs a connection. • Fonts load from Google Fonts with system fallbacks. 12. Charts and visualisation Charts included • Temperature history: maximum surface temperature in kelvin, two sites compared. • Atmospheric pressure graph in pascals, two sites compared. • Wind-condition chart in metres per second, two sites compared. • Dust opacity chart across the chosen range, two sites compared. • Elevation profile in km along each planner route. • Route distance comparison as bars, in km. • Resource evidence comparison: ice sites counted by class. • Simulated solar power across the Mars year against the habitat load, in kW. • Simulated survival reserves over the run: battery percent, water days and food days. • Mission exploration timeline: a ten-event list from Mariner 4 in 1965 to Perseverance and Zhurong in 2021. Chart controls • Choose Site A and Site B from the catalogue. • Choose a range of 30 sols, 90 sols or one Mars year. • Move a start-sol slider from 0 to 668. • Hover to see the value of each series at that position. Chart design • Drawn on a canvas with one shared scale for marks, ticks and labels. • A faint grid and labeled axes. • Every chart title shows its unit in brackets. • The last point of each line is emphasized. • A legend names each series when there is more than one. • Weather charts carry a note that the source is a demonstration model and that the sols are model sols, not mission dates. • Colors are chosen to stay distinct in lightness as well as hue. Limits • Comparing real observations from different missions needs live data, which is not connected. • The timeline is a list and not a drawn chart. 13. Architecture and technology Prototype technology • Plain JavaScript and CSS in one HTML file. • Three.js release 128 for the 3D globe. • HTML canvas for the 2D map and all charts. • Google Fonts: Space Grotesk and IBM Plex Mono. • Browser local storage for bookmarks and recent items. • No backend and no database. Production technology named in the brief • React or an equivalent framework, with TypeScript. • CSS with a reusable design system. • Three.js or CesiumJS for 3D visualisation. • MapLibre or another mapping library. • Plotly or an equivalent charting library. • Python with FastAPI and structured data-processing modules. • Geospatial processing libraries. • PostgreSQL with PostGIS for saved locations and mission plans. • GeoJSON for features and raster and elevation formats for imagery. • Local caching for frequently used data. • Capacitor for the Android application. The nine modules in the brief and where each stands • User interface: navigation rail, panels, search and responsive layout are built. • 3D Mars visualisation: built with Three.js and a 2D canvas map. • Mapping and geographic data: built as a catalogue and great-circle math. GeoJSON and tiles are planned. • NASA data integration: not built. A data-sources page lists each intended source and its status. • Scientific information management: built as five data classes on every record. • Mission planning: built with three modeled routes and a report. • Survival simulation: built with five simulation modules. • Data visualisation: built with canvas charts. • User settings and saved missions: bookmarks only, in the browser. Status of intended data sources • NASA Planetary Data System: not connected. • NASA Mars Trek: not connected. • MRO HiRISE, CRISM and SHARAD: not connected. • Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter elevation: replaced by the demonstration terrain model. • Curiosity REMS and Perseverance MEDA weather: replaced by the weather simulation. • Mars Odyssey and Mars Express: represented only through catalogue entries. • Live calls to these services are blocked inside the hosted page, so a backend proxy is needed. Android plan • Put the HTML file in the www folder of a Capacitor project. • Run npx cap add android, then npx cap sync. • Controls are sized for touch and panels stack on narrow screens. • The globe supports drag and pinch. • The Android app itself is not built. 14. Testing and verification Checks completed • Every script in the page parses without syntax errors in Node. • A terrain test over 20,000 random points gave heights from about minus 7.0 to plus 19.4 km. • Olympus Mons measured about plus 19.6 km and Hellas Planitia about minus 6.6 km in the model. • A route test between the proposed habitats near Jezero and Gale gave three routes: 3,736 km direct and 4,036 km for each detour. • Travel times for those routes were 77.8 sols and 84.1 sols at 8 km per hour and 6 hours per sol. • Solar test at 18 degrees north: about 110 W per square meter at the surface in normal dust and solar longitude 90. • Solar test under heavy dust of 4.0 at solar longitude 250: about 27 W per square meter, a drop of about three quarters. • The 13-page presentation PDF was rendered and inspected, and two layout faults were found and fixed. • Fault one: text on the vision slide ran into the footer, fixed by reducing the headline size. • Fault two: card headings on the limits slide were unreadable on a dark card, fixed with a color rule. • The PDF copy uses substitute fonts, so headings look slightly different from the online deck. Still to do • Open the page in current Chrome, Safari and Firefox and confirm the globe, panels and charts draw correctly. • Test touch gestures, pinch zoom and panel stacking on real phones. • Run an accessibility check for contrast, keyboard use and screen-reader labels. • Compare every catalogue coordinate and elevation with NASA, USGS or ESA references. • Compare modeled temperatures, pressures and routes with mission data once real datasets are connected. • Have a domain expert review the survival formulas. • Measure load time and performance on low-end phones. • Test behavior with the network off and with the 3D library blocked. 15. Limitations and risks Limitations • Terrain and elevation are a procedural model. The globe resembles Mars but is not NASA imagery. Remedy: load MOLA elevation and HiRISE or Mars Trek tiles. • There is no live NASA data. Weather and rover readings are simulated. Remedy: a backend that fetches, caches and flags stale observations. • The catalogue was written from general knowledge. Coordinates and descriptions may contain errors. Remedy: verify every record against NASA, USGS or ESA sources. • Routes use coarse slope and a constant speed. Travel times are rough and hazards can be missed. Remedy: route over real slope and roughness rasters with a vehicle model. • Survival formulas are simplified. Results show trends and not engineering values. Remedy: expert review and calibrated models. • Bookmarks live in one browser. They do not follow the user to another device. Remedy: accounts and a saved-missions database. • The hosted page cannot print or download. Reports are copied as text. Remedy: export from the production build. • The Android app is not built. Remedy: wrap the front end with Capacitor. • The interface has not been tested in browsers and on phones. Layout or gesture faults may exist. Remedy: run the testing plan in section 14. • No real photographs or before-and-after image comparisons are shown, because remote images cannot load in the hosted page. The discoveries page links to NASA sources instead. • No drag-to-measure ruler exists. • The brief's section 14 on performance, security and reliability was cut off, so it is not addressed. Risks and mitigations • Risk: a user mistakes simulated data for real data. Mitigation: class tags, banners and consistent labels on every simulated value. • Risk: a possible resource is read as an accessible supply. Mitigation: evidence classes and wording that never calls a possible deposit a supply. • Risk: a route is read as safe. Mitigation: routes are never labeled safe and are always labeled modeled. • Risk: survival results are used operationally. Mitigation: a standing statement that it is not a life-support or safety system. • Risk: the 3D library fails to load from the network. Mitigation: automatic fallback to the 2D map, and bundling the library in the production build. 16. Roadmap and future work Phase 1: Real terrain • Add MOLA elevation and imagery tiles from NASA Mars Trek and HiRISE. • Compute slope and roughness from real rasters. • Show real before-and-after image comparisons. Phase 2: Live and archived weather • Fetch and cache Curiosity REMS and Perseverance MEDA series. • Show observation time and freshness on every value. • Flag outdated readings. • Compare real observations from different missions where that is scientifically appropriate. Phase 3: Saved missions • Add accounts. • Save plans and bookmarks in PostgreSQL with PostGIS. • Create shareable mission links. Phase 4: Better routing • Route over slope and hazard rasters. • Add a vehicle and crew model. • Compare modeled routes with real rover drive logs. • Add a drag-to-measure distance tool. Phase 5: Android • Wrap the front end with Capacitor. • Cache data for weak networks. • Test on real devices. Phase 6: Hardening • Address the unfinished section 14 of the brief. • Set performance budgets. • Run a security review. • Improve error handling and offline behavior. Production stack • React with TypeScript on the front end. • A FastAPI service in Python for data processing and caching. • GeoJSON and raster formats for geographic data. 17. Conclusion Outcome • A single page brings a 3D globe, seven map layers, route planning and a survival simulation together. • A clear line is kept between what is known about Mars and what is only modeled. • Four of the brief's eight goals are fully met and four are partly met. • The main contribution is the labeling discipline: five data classes, graded ice evidence, modeled route labels, and a standing refusal to call a route safe or a possible deposit a water supply. Main weaknesses • The physical numbers are demonstration models. • The interface has not yet been tested in real browsers and on phones. • Catalogue coordinates have not been verified against NASA sources. Deliverables produced • The web prototype, as one HTML file. • A 13-slide presentation: cover, vision, explorer, layers, data labels, dashboard, planner, survival, charts, architecture, limits, roadmap and closing. • A PDF copy of the presentation. • A project report with an executive summary. • This detailed point-by-point report.
